articles.title: 5 ChatGPT prompts worth stealing for your business
articles.excerpt: Not generic tips — prompts tested on real entrepreneur cases.
body: Most prompts floating around are too vague to be useful. Here are five that give a usable result on the first try.
1. "Act as a skeptical customer and raise 5 objections to this offer: [describe the offer]." — to stress-test an offer before publishing it.
2. "Summarize these 10 customer reviews into 3 recurring themes, with one quote for each." — to turn scattered feedback into a real decision.
3. "Rewrite this message for a reader with 10 seconds, not 2 minutes." — for anything going out on WhatsApp or a story.
4. "List the 5 questions a customer would ask before buying [product], and answer each in one sentence." — the base of a good FAQ.
5. "Turn these notes into 3 distinct LinkedIn posts, each with a different angle." — to stop staring at a blank page.
The common thread: each prompt gives the AI a precise role and a format constraint. That's what separates a generic answer from a usable one.

articles.title: Meta Ads on a small budget: what actually works
articles.excerpt: With $20 a day, here's where to put it — and where definitely not to.
body: With a small budget, the most common mistake is trying to reach everyone. Broad targeting dilutes every dollar spent.
First rule: one goal, one campaign. Don't mix awareness and conversion in the same campaign — the algorithm optimizes for a single signal at a time.
Second rule: let a campaign run for at least 3 to 4 days before judging results. Cutting it too early stops the algorithm from finding its audience.
Third rule: a good visual beats good targeting. With a small budget, invest the time you save on targeting into a visual that stops the scroll.
Finally, measure cost per result, not just reach. A campaign that reaches fewer people but converts better stays more profitable.

articles.title: Why your brand needs exactly one word
articles.excerpt: Brands that try to say everything end up saying nothing. Here's how to find the one word that matters.
body: Ask ten people to describe your brand in one word. If you get ten different answers, that's not a communication problem — it's a positioning problem.
A strong brand owns exactly one word in its customer's mind: fast, accessible, premium, local. Everything else — tone, visuals, pricing — should serve that word, not compete with it.
To find it: list everything your brand could claim, then cross out anything a competitor could claim too. What's left is your word.
It's not a tagline. It's the filter that should guide every brand decision from here on.

articles.title: Mobile money: what it changes about your sales funnel
articles.excerpt: Mobile payment isn't just another option — it changes how you build the whole funnel.
body: A funnel built for card payment doesn't work as-is for mobile money — payment habits are different, and the funnel needs to adapt.
First, the price needs to be visible before any friction: no form to fill out before seeing the final amount in USD or local currency.
Second, payment should stay inside the app or the conversation as much as possible — every external redirect loses customers.
Finally, always confirm payment receipt with an immediate message, even a basic one. Uncertainty about "did it work?" is the top cause of drop-off right after payment.
Mobile money isn't a secondary payment method tacked on at the end — it's a starting point to design the funnel around.
